paragraphs: The spear barring the camp gate did not move.

Mist still clung to the tips of the grass on Xiliu Plain. Fu Hong reined in his horse. Beyond the palisade he heard restless horses shifting in their lines, and from time to time a long neigh pierced the morning air. The young sentry studied the pass hanging from the prince’s belt, turned it over, and rubbed the vermilion seal with his thumb.
“I am not authorized to inspect this,” he said. “You’ll have to wait for my company leader.”

Fu Hong nodded. His guards from the Eastern Palace had flushed with anger, but he raised a hand before they could scold the soldier. A moment later the company leader came running and dropped to his knees so abruptly that mud splashed over them. Only then did the sentry realize he had stopped the crown prince. His spear trembled in his hands.

“Get up.” Fu Hong held out a hand. “You could not identify a pass issued by the Department of State Affairs, but you held your post. That is not your mistake. Before the day is out, have the different offices send copies of their approved seals and passes to every camp gate.”
The sentry remained kneeling, his gaze fixed on the horse’s hooves.

Fu Hong rode past him into the camp. New wooden fences stood in rows, but all the banners hanging from them were old: red standards, black ones, and little white-edged pennons once carried by Yan cavalry. The dozen or so encampments were separated by unfinished trenches. Men guarded their own piles of fodder and grain like villagers newly arrived from every quarter, who had happened to settle on the same plain. The shouting ahead grew louder.

Several hundred men had gathered on either bank of the northern canal. The Di troops had arrived first and occupied the higher ground near the water, driving their palisade posts deep. Xianbei cavalrymen had come only during the night. They stood holding their horses on the low ground, still wet with dew, where the hooves sank into mud. Officers on both sides brandished orders for camp placement and neither would yield.

“I came according to the central army’s plan,” said Helai Ba, a Xianbei cavalry officer. He had learned to ride in the armies of Yan in his youth, and his voice was deep and impatient. “The north bank belongs to the cavalry. Are our horses to spend the winter in a swamp because fog came down last night?”
The Di commandant pressed a hand against the gate of the enclosure. “The deputy commander has issued a new order. If you object, take it to Lord Fu.”
“Which Lord Fu?”
Several old soldiers behind the barrier drew their swords a finger’s breadth at the question. From his horse Fu Hong put out a hand. “Bring me both orders.”

One bore the vermilion seal of the central army; the other was handwritten by Fu Chong. They were dated barely half a day apart. Fu Hong had the construction officer guide him along the canal. On the north slope, where the earth had not yet been leveled, seven or eight survey stakes stood, though some had already been pulled out. The mud was stamped with hoofprints. The deepest tracks led toward the Di camp.
“How many horses can this higher ground accommodate?” he asked.
“About six thousand,” the construction officer replied.
“And how many have these two units brought?”
“Just over twenty-eight hundred Di cavalry and thirty-one hundred Xianbei.”

“Then what is there to quarrel about?” Fu Hong pointed toward the northern slope. “Remove part of the fence. Leave a horse lane for each unit. Place their troughs at different points along the canal, and have the company leaders on both sides record the water drawn. Not one horse needs moving out today.”
The Di commandant’s face changed. “Are we to share a camp with them?”
“Not a tent. Begin by sharing a ditch of water,” Fu Hong said. “If there is not enough, I shall remain here today and hear which horse died of thirst first.”

Someone among the Xianbei laughed. An old Di soldier flung the timber in his hands onto the mud with a heavy thud. Helai Ba set a foot on it and called his men over to help lift it. Neither side thanked the other, but at last they shifted part of the crossbar out of the way.

By noon Fu Hong could scarcely find his ten clerks. One had gone to write down the names of wounded men in an outlying camp; another was squatting beside a cookfire counting rations. One had taken a wrong turning at a gate and been asked six times what people he belonged to. When the prince gathered them again, their sleeves were smeared with ink, mud, and horsehair. Compared with the old records from the Department of State Affairs, the rolls they had drawn up differed by more than two hundred names on the very first day.
The bells on a horse’s harness sounded outside the central command tent late that afternoon. Murong Chui had arrived.

He had brought none of the old bodyguards who had followed him from Yan. His twenty escorts came from several units, their armor and helmets ill-matched. Yet the Xianbei veterans standing by the entrance involuntarily straightened when they saw him. Someone in the crowd murmured, “Prince of Wu.” An old cavalryman with a long scar on his left cheek stepped out and bent both knees.
“Helai Yan, once of the Left Valiant Cavalry of Yan, greets the Prince of Wu.”
Murong Chui pulled his horse to a halt.

When the old soldier looked up, his eyes were wet. More than ten years earlier, on an autumn hunt in Youzhou, Murong Chui had led them fighting back out of a mountain hollow. Helai Yan had taken a spear thrust meant for him, and the scar was what remained. Across years and mountains, the old world had risen again on this unfamiliar plain.
Murong Chui dismounted and helped him to his feet.
“You’re still alive.”
Helai Yan’s lips trembled. “I am, my lord. But Yan ...”
Murong Chui glanced at him, then at the new unit badge on his arm.
“Who commands your company?”
“Helai Ba.”
“And what is my present military title?”
“Champion General.”
“Then use it.”

Helai Yan hesitated and made no reply. Murong Chui did not press him. Instead, he ordered the old standards at the gates taken down. When the soldiers heard that even the red banners of the founding Di units were to be removed, some protested at once. Murong Chui simply called for the new unit flags prepared by the central army and ordered the standard of the First Battalion hoisted on its timber platform. The Qin banner went up awkwardly; twice the rope tangled around the freshly cut pole. Only after much hauling did it finally spread in the wind.

Fu Chong arrived at dusk with three hundred personal guards. Their armor plates matched perfectly, and the bronze wolf-fang fittings on their saddles gleamed in the fading light. He rode past the dismantled fence and straight into the main tent. Before taking so much as a drink of water, he opened the officers' roster.
“Why has Helai Ba been given the Third Cavalry Company?” he asked.
“He knows cavalry warfare,” Murong Chui said.
“Are there no Di sons who know how to ride?”
“There are.”
“Yet you chose him?”
“Two Di commanders already lead cavalry companies. Give all three to your men and there is no place left for Helai Ba’s.”
Fu Chong shut the register and looked up. “You sound as if you are dividing fields between the different peoples.”
Murong Chui gave a faint smile. “Fields have boundaries. If cavalry companies draw boundaries between themselves when battle comes, who will hold the line?”
Fu Chong let that pass and turned to Fu Hong. “Does Your Highness approve?”

Fu Hong was recording the discrepancies in the morning’s muster in the margin of his book. He set down his brush. “The assignments have been issued. We will follow them during the six-month trial. If any officer proves unfit, let both generals submit a report. His name will not be changed merely for his ancestry.”
Fu Chong watched him for a long moment. “The old servants of the Fu family taught your father to keep accounts that way when he was a boy.”

Fu Hong heard the barb, but he would not discard what lay beneath it. Fu Chong had lost two sons in Bingzhou and Hejian. The widows of his former soldiers still came to his house for relief. He resisted giving up his men, yet some of those men had genuinely entrusted their lives to him.
“The unpaid relief is still under investigation,” Fu Hong said. “I shall keep a copy of your old rolls. Whatever is verified will be paid by the court.”
Fu Chong looked ready to say more. In the end he merely nodded.
The First Battalion lit its cooking fires. Trouble rose first from the meat broth.

Following their old units' customs, the ration officer gave whole cuts of mutton to the Di cavalry. The Xianbei received a few bones; the Han Chinese foot soldiers got two extra measures of millet. When the Qiang arrived last, only a basket of musty grain remained at the storehouse door. A young Qiang archer named Manu emptied it onto the ground, sending kernels rolling into the mud. He cursed in Qiang for a long time. The storehouse clerks understood nothing, but when someone said he was insulting their mothers, they immediately called for soldiers to bind him.

Before the cudgels fell, Murong Chui arrived. He tasted the millet first, chewed twice, and spat it out. Then he ordered every ration book opened. The mutton had been brought by the Di themselves, not yet priced or reimbursed, yet it had also been entered once among the government’s grain and provisions. The Xianbei meat was old stock. The Qiang’s basket of millet had originally been set aside as horse feed.
“Who entered the mutton in the accounts?” Murong Chui asked.
A supply officer knelt but still tried to defend himself. “The Di brought it. Naturally the Di should eat it.”
“Count it, issue a receipt, and have the army reimburse them later,” Murong Chui said. “But if the pot is in one camp today, everyone in that camp must have something fit to eat.”
Fu Chong heard what was happening and came to the warehouse. “Would the general make himself beloved by giving away my sheep?”
“If your sheep have merely been lent to the army, they must of course be repaid. But if they are already entered as public provisions while only your men receive the meat, I am bound to investigate.”
Fu Chong glanced at the moldy grain scattered in the mud. His expression darkened, and he said no more in the supply officer’s defense.

That night several great pots of millet boiled together in the camp. The mutton had been cut so small that five men shared one ladleful, and no one could taste the cooking of his old home. The Di complained there was too little meat. The Xianbei grumbled that the beans were undercooked. Manu found a kernel of moldy millet in his bowl and nearly threw the bowl away. But Zhao An, a Han Chinese soldier, hooked a sheep bone from the pot and passed it to Zhai Hei, a burly Dingling man beside him, gesturing at his teeth to show him how to gnaw it. Zhai Hei took it and cracked it between his teeth. Everyone at the table laughed.

Murong Chui passed the cookfires, heard the quarrels still breaking out on every side, and slowly let himself breathe amid the steam of the porridge. At least tonight everyone had something to complain about.

By the next morning, however, the drill ground had nearly become a place of death. The central army’s drums, the cavalry horns, and the whistles familiar to Qiang archers could not all be replaced overnight. The Han Chinese infantry had held their shields high for some time while the Xianbei horsemen still waited for the horn. When dust from the slope concealed the signal flag, the Qiang archers thought the cavalry were charging their own formation. Arrows went to strings. Even Murong Chui’s messenger did not dare run forward.

After three days, the drums, horns, and flags could at last be made to agree, more or less. Murong Chui ordered the whole camp to learn just three commands: advance, halt, withdraw. Other tactics were left to the units that knew how to use them. The arts of mounted archery had been honed in the snows of Liaodong. Putting the men into new armor would not make them forget what their hands knew.

On the fourth day Fu Chong personally formed the Di cavalry beside the central command. When the exercise reached the point at which Xianbei horsemen were to circle around the infantry, he suddenly ordered his retainers to sound an old call.
The shrill horn split the autumn sky.

Thousands of Di cavalrymen swung their horses around. They obeyed a signal familiar for twenty years: turn back to guard the commander’s tent. The Xianbei cavalry kept charging forward. The two waves of horses met in a narrow camp road. Horses reared in the front ranks; those behind could not rein in. The shield-bearing infantry fell into confusion. A Qiang arrow struck a horse in the neck, and the wounded animal plunged, screaming, into the foot soldiers. Dust engulfed the field, mingled with the cries of men.

Murong Chui galloped to the raised command platform. With his own hands he cut the cord holding a side banner and ordered the halt drum beaten. The rapid strokes followed one another until the cavalry began to disentangle themselves from the trampled mud. When the physicians arrived, thirty-seven men were injured. A young Han Chinese soldier’s leg had been broken beneath a horse; the jagged bone showed through his trousers. He wept and screamed for his mother on the stretcher. Nothing in that voice sounded like military glory.
Fu Chong sat his horse and looked at Murong Chui. “Now do you understand why the old signals cannot be changed?”
“And you have seen what happens when they are not changed,” Murong Chui answered.
“I sounded the call to guard the commander. On a real battlefield, would you wait for the enemy to explain your new rules?”
“There is no enemy here.”
“There will be.”

Fu Hong came toward them through the wounded. Fresh blood marked his boots. He first asked the military law officer who had established the signals for the day’s exercise. When he had heard the answer, he turned to Fu Chong. “Did you inform the commander beforehand?”
“No.”
“Did you know the two wings did not recognize that call?”
“Yes.”
“And you sounded it anyway?”
“Your Highness needed to see it for yourself.”

Fu Hong looked at the pale face of the young soldier on the stretcher. The broken leg was said to be grave, and the man no longer dared ask whether he would ever ride again. Several times the prince opened his mouth, but he would not make anger his answer.

“Thirty-seven wounded today. The army will advance the costs of medicine, leave from service, and compensation for any lasting injury. General Fu changed the signal without authority and caused these casualties. Record the offense and report it to His Majesty under military law. Once his share is assessed, recover the damages from his stipend and estate. If he changes an order without permission again, remove him first from the deputy command and send the case to the Court of Judicial Review.”
The mockery slowly left Fu Chong’s face. “Is Your Highness afraid to be known as the man who killed one of the founding veterans?”
“I am afraid the wounded cannot wait for the court to finish arguing.” Fu Hong pointed to the young soldier with the shattered leg. “He needs medicine today.”

He then asked Fu Chong to surrender all the old Di cavalry signals for translation and trial by the central army. Fu Chong remained unconvinced, but at last he unfastened the horn at his waist and placed it on the table. Long use had worn a shallow groove around its mouthpiece. On the inner curve Fu Hong noticed two small characters: the name of Fu Chong’s eldest son, long dead. He said no more harsh words.

That night Murong Chui did not return to the main tent. He went instead to the smaller tents and the ration sheds, where the noise was greater than on the drill ground. The construction officers assigned sleeping mats to five men per tent, the grain clerks issued grain in groups of ten, and the night patrols still called the roll according to the old twenty-man units. If one man disappeared, it seemed every register in the camp had to be consulted.

An old soldier complained about being mustered in the middle of the night. He had taken his four tentmates with him to draw their evening food and asked the patrolman to mark them all present on a single wooden tally. The grain clerk standing nearby said it would save steps. Murong Chui borrowed the sweat-darkened tally; its back was still smudged with soot from a cooking pot.
“Try it for thirty tents,” he said. “Mix men from different former camps in each. Record anyone who objects. We will see how it works after ten days.”
No one thought it much of a change. Yet those thirty tents were lively indeed.

Zhao An was assigned to a tent with Liang Hu, Helai Yan, Manu, and Zhai Hei. Liang Hu, twenty-seven, was the finest horseman among them and had ridden into Hedong with Fu Chong’s old army. Helai Yan had served longer; no one dared ask about the scar on his face. Manu carried a case of bamboo arrows and knew only two commands in Chinese, “halt” and “loose.” Zhai Hei was so strong that he routinely carried an extra grain sack for others, yet he could not follow a single argument spoken around him.

At first the company leader proposed Liang Hu as head of the five-man squad. Helai Yan objected that he had served longer than twice Liang Hu’s lifetime. Liang Hu laughed in his face. “Yan’s been dead for years. You still want credit for seniority?”

They nearly came to blows. Zhao An rushed between them and was kicked to the ground. Murong Chui finally had each man demonstrate his skill. Liang Hu rode well; Helai Yan knew the night watch; Manu was a keen archer; no man in the squad could carry a load like Zhai Hei. Then came reading the signal flags and verifying rations. The other four watched Zhao An work through an entire scroll without difficulty, and for once no one argued over who was best.
“For the first month, rotate the post,” Murong Chui ruled. “When trouble comes, obey whoever is serving as squad leader. If anything goes wrong, I shall question that man first.”

That evening the five quarreled again, this time over sleeping places. Zhao An fetched a long stick and measured the mats one by one. He stood the stick in the corner. “Take an extra foot and you’ll scrub everyone’s pots tomorrow.” Manu understood little of the words, but Zhao An’s gestures made him grin. Zhai Hei deliberately stretched his feet over the boundary and nearly earned a punch from Liang Hu.

In the middle of the night Zhao An began to snore, shaking dust from the tent roof. No one could wake him. The next day his boots were missing, and he had to run barefoot across half the muddy camp looking for the culprit. Every man denied knowing anything, though Zhai Hei laughed so hard that bean soup sprayed from his mouth.

But their real troubles were not the kind they could laugh at. One evening Liang Hu slipped away to drink in his old Di camp. The other four, as the new rules required, reported that he had failed to return to his tent. When Liang Hu came back, he rounded on Helai Yan. “You informed against me?”
“I went looking for you,” Helai Yan said. “When the night patrol asked who was missing, I couldn’t even say whether you were alive.”

Liang Hu drew his short sword a finger’s breadth. Helai Yan’s hand went to his own hilt. Zhao An seized Liang Hu around the waist, Manu shoved Helai Yan away, and Zhai Hei simply knocked both men down. In the end Liang Hu was ordered to clean the stables for three days; for one of those days the other four had to help him carry the manure baskets.
On the first day Liang Hu cursed as he shoveled. Helai Yan sat nearby sharpening a blade. It was Liang Hu’s old short sword, with a little wolf-fang carving on the end of the hilt.
“Why are you touching my sword?” Liang Hu demanded.
“The edge had curled.”
“That’s none of your business.”
Helai Yan tossed it onto the straw mat. “Then don’t use it.”

Liang Hu picked it up and tested the blade. The edge shone cleanly. He had almost thanked him, but one look at Helai Yan’s scarred face stopped the words. When the older man had gone, Liang Hu weighed the sword once or twice in his palm and hung it back on the wooden post inside the tent.

On the twelfth day of the trial a man from another squad deserted during the night. His four tentmates, afraid their grain would be withheld, lied that he was sick in the infirmary. When Murong Chui heard, he abolished the old rule that deprived an entire squad of rations whenever one man was absent. Only those who knowingly concealed an absence would be punished; grain would be issued to those actually present, with the missing soldier entered separately. One line of regulation had been rewritten, and the night patrol’s account book gained two more. The clerks complained, but even as they complained, they made the changes.

After half a month, a combined exercise was at last completed, though barely. At the flag signal the infantry formed a shield wall, the archers came forward as ordered, and the Di and Xianbei horsemen wheeled around the two flanks. The formation was uneven and some still mistook the drumbeats. Thirty thousand men moved with an almost maddening slowness. But this time not a single horse plunged into their own infantry.

On the command platform, Fu Chong heard one note of the central army’s old horn, and a muscle shifted faintly in his cheek. He looked toward his former soldiers. Several cavalrymen glanced back at him, but then turned toward the main standard. Liang Hu, riding among them, instinctively checked his horse. Helai Yan caught his bridle and pointed to the Qin flag. Through clenched teeth Liang Hu followed the new order. Manu raised his bow at the wrong moment and Zhao An pushed it down; Zhai Hei fell behind under his arrow cases, and Liang Hu wheeled back to carry one of the bags for him. The five cursed and quarreled all the way across the field, but none was left behind.

When the inspection ended, Fu Hong tapped the empty water clock with his knuckles and slowly let out his breath. Murong Chui was still studying the broken tracks the troops had left on the exercise ground.
“Are you displeased, General?” Fu Hong asked.
“Still too slow. In an ambush, that one moment of delay would be enough to bury an entire battalion.”
“At least they did not trample their own men today.”
Only then did Murong Chui nod. “That much can be written down.”

At dusk the camp smelled of millet cooking, and soldiers gathered around the pots to share their food. Liang Hu complained that the meat was so scarce the new army had divided the sheep until even its shadow had vanished. Helai Yan laughed and told him to go steal some from the deputy commander’s tent if he was so capable. Manu heard the word “sheep” and laughed before anyone else. In the commotion Zhai Hei scooped the last bone from the bottom of the pot; Zhao An struck at his hand with his chopsticks and missed.

After dark Helai Yan went out alone. He said he wanted to see a horse that had fallen sick beyond the western palisade and collect a bridle he had sent for repair. Zhao An was checking the night roll and acknowledged him without looking up. Liang Hu sat on his straw mat polishing his scabbard and did not lift his head.

Late that night the patrol found a body in a field ditch northwest of the camp. The man lay on his back in the mud, blood soaking the left side of his chest, sticky earth clinging to the back of his head. A deep cut split his left palm. In his right he still clutched a handful of grass tangled with strands of black mane. The men carrying the lantern first saw the old scar on his left cheek and recoiled.
“Helai Yan.”

A short sword was trapped beneath his body. When the lantern light fell on it, they saw the wolf-fang carving on the hilt. Some of the guards recognized the pattern: it belonged to Fu Chong’s old army, and it was the sword they had seen at Liang Hu’s side during the day.

After the first beat of the night watch drum, the news reached the Xianbei camp. By the second, Di soldiers were running over to ask. By the third, the body had been lifted onto a door panel, and the wolf-fang sword had passed through dozens of hands. Every man now claimed to have seen it with his own eyes.
Liang Hu came out of his tent and reached for the sword at his waist. His empty scabbard knocked lightly against his leg.

He remembered Helai Yan laughing that afternoon and telling him to steal mutton, and the blade passing back and forth over the older man’s whetstone. Now it lay beside the dead man, cold as though it had never rested in Liang Hu’s hand.
A torch flared at the far end of the camp road. Then a second, and a third.
Soon the torches had gathered into two opposing banks of fire.
